extracted.intended_audience: journalists, Reuters reporters and editors, news writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and usage rules for writing and editing news copy for Reuters, covering naming, terminology, grammar, punctuation, capitalization, numeric rounding and sensitive-topic usage. Intended to standardize Reuters output for a global audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICRC naming at first reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the ICRC title in full at first reference; do not abbreviate to the 'International Red Cross’ since such a body does not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For brevity in a lead you can refer to a Red Cross official or spokesman but make clear later which organisation he or she belongs to. See www.icrc.org and www.ifrc.org.

rubrics_metrics.name: refer vs allude
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer means to mention directly. Allude means to refer in passing without making an explicit mention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct verb: He alluded to the sins of his past and referred to his criminal record.

rubrics_metrics.name: refute (use with care)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refute means to disprove, not to deny or reject. Rebut has a similar meaning, not just to argue against, so its use implies an editorial judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using refute/rebut except in quotes or unless you are sure they are correct; prefer deny or reject when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: regime (avoid negative overtones)
rubrics_metrics.description: A word with negative overtones in a political context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use government instead of regime in most contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: register office wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'register office', not 'registry office'.

rubrics_metrics.name: reins vs reigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Reins control a horse. A monarch reigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: reiterate again (avoid tautology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reiterate again is a tautology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Just 'reiterate' will do.

rubrics_metrics.name: relatively (use only in comparisons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'relatively' unless in a comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague phrases like 'He is relatively young.' Instead write 'He is younger than the rest of the team.'

rubrics_metrics.name: religion and religious titles (capitalisation and first reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalise names of divinities and capitalise religious titles when they immediately precede a personal name; otherwise use lower case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only the simplest and best-known titles at first reference (e.g. the Rev. Jesse Jackson, Dr John Smith rather than the Right Rev. John Smith). Capitalise names of denominations and religious movements (Baptist, Buddhist, Christian, Church of England, Islamic, Jew, Jewish, Muslim, Orthodox). Use lower case for non-denominational references (e.g. adult baptism, orthodox beliefs).

rubrics_metrics.name: religious terms: usage and definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferred forms and short definitions for many religious terms and group names, with guidance on sensitive or misleading descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and rules include: abaya (full-body overgarment); adhan (Muslim call to prayer); Anglican Communion (use that name, not 'Worldwide'); Baha'i faith (do not describe as an offshoot of Islam; avoid implying origin); basilica (major church with special status); burqa (one-piece covering; avoid other-language misuses); cardinal (honorary title for clerics; indicate age rule for conclave); cathedral (central church of a diocese); chador (cloak leaving face visible, mostly Iran); Christian (use as overall term but prefer precise denomination); church/Church (church = building or denomination; capitalise in titles); Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (give official title soon after 'Mormon church'); cult (use very carefully); denomination (use precise name where possible); Eastern Catholic churches (term defined); ecumenism vs inter-faith (distinguish); Episcopal Church/terms (do not call members 'Episcopals'); evangelical (capitalize only in titles; explain regional differences); evangelism/proselytise (use neutral/avoid negative connotations); evangelist/ministers/priest titles (use Rev. rather than Father except in quotes; use actual titles); fundamentalist (avoid where overused); Haj (capitalise); headscarf/hijab/niqab (distinguish terms); Mass (celebrated or said); Methodist churches (distinguish family of churches); minister (not a title—do not capitalise); Monsignor (better avoided—use actual title); new religious movement (neutral term); Orthodox/orthodox (capitalize in titles); pontiff/Pope (capitalisation rules); proselytise vs evangelise (connotations); Roman Catholic Church (official title). Avoid pejorative nicknames (e.g. 'Moonie') and explain contested or sensitive points (e.g. Baha'i treatment in Iran).

rubrics_metrics.name: religious leadership titles and papal references
rubrics_metrics.description: How to refer to the pope, cardinals and other church hierarchy, and how to use Roman numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to a reigning pope at first reference as 'Pope Benedict' and subsequently as 'the pope' or 'the pontiff'. A reigning pope does not take Roman numerals after his name in Reuters copy unless omitting them would cause confusion. Past church leaders should take Roman numerals on first reference (e.g. Pope Pius XII) and may be referred to by their name subsequently. For cardinals and other prelates: 'At first reference Cardinal John Doe. At subsequent references the cardinal or Doe.' Prefer avoiding 'monsignor'; use Rev. for priests except in quotes. Explain Curia and distinguish Vatican (city-state) and Holy See (Church administration) when necessary; papal envoys are papal nuncios and embassies are nunciatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: reluctant vs reticent
rubrics_metrics.description: Reluctant means unwilling or resisting. Reticent means sparing in communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the correct word: a gossip is reluctant to be reticent.

rubrics_metrics.name: remain/ remained (avoid in leads)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'remain' in leads; there is usually a more lively phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: remainder wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'the rest' rather than 'remainder'.

rubrics_metrics.name: rendezvous usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Rendezvous is both singular and plural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer meeting or appointment where clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: repeat vs repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: The noun is 'repetition', the verb is 'repeat'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'repetition' for the noun: John Smith tried to avoid a repetition of his blunder, not a repeat of his blunder.

rubrics_metrics.name: repechage (sports definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: In sport, a contest between runners-up, usually for a place in the final (especially in rowing).

rubrics_metrics.name: replica definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Replica means an exact reproduction, in size and materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse with 'model'.

rubrics_metrics.name: reported/reportedly sourcing rule
rubrics_metrics.description: If you use the word 'reported' without stating the source at once, you must give it in the next sentence or paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'reportedly'.

rubrics_metrics.name: report vs report on
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'report on', not 'report into'.

rubrics_metrics.name: reports (specify source)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not refer just to 'reports'—specify where the reports come from or originate.

rubrics_metrics.name: requirements vs needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'needs' as the shorter and better word than 'requirements' where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: reveal (use with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the word 'reveal' implies acceptance that the statement is true and that the information had previously been kept secret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: revenue (singular)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'revenue' not 'revenues'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverend and religious titles capitalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalise religious titles when they immediately precede a personal name, otherwise use lower case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the simplest and best-known titles at first reference, e.g. the Rev. Jesse Jackson, Dr John Smith rather than the Right Rev. John Smith.

rubrics_metrics.name: revert back (avoid redundancy)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Revert back' is redundant; use 'revert'.

rubrics_metrics.name: rounding figures (numeric rounding rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on how to round numbers in copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Round off unwieldy figures (e.g. Japan produced 1.45 million cars rather than 1,453,123). As a rule round off millions to the nearest 10,000, thousands to the nearest 100, hundreds to the nearest 10. Figures are normally rounded to two significant decimals, with halves rounded upwards. Do not round interest rates—give them to the full number of decimal places supplied by the source. Round foreign exchange quotations to four decimal places. Do not round company dividends; give them to the full number of decimal places supplied by the source. If a country adjusts its currency, any rate given must not be rounded. Where totals do not add up because of rounding, explain it.

rubrics_metrics.name: row (do not use for dispute)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use 'row' to mean argument or dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid this British informal usage in contexts where it may confuse international readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: royalty references and Roman numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain the titles of rulers and their consorts at second reference; use Roman numerals for royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g. King Hussein, Queen Beatrix, the queen. Use Roman numerals like Charles I, Louis XIV not Charles 1st or Charles the First. At first reference use full titles (Prince Charles, Prince of Wales), then Charles or the prince subsequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: rubber stamp hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use two words as a noun, hyphenated as a verb or adjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: rubber stamp (noun) vs rubber-stamp (verb/adjective).

rubrics_metrics.name: rule (political wording)
rubrics_metrics.description: In political contexts 'rule' has negative overtones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'govern' as a verb instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: run for office vs stand
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'run for office' for presidential candidates; for parliamentary candidates use 'stand'.

rubrics_metrics.name: rundown/run down distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Rundown is the noun (prefer review or summary). The verb is 'run down' and the adjective is 'run-down'.

rubrics_metrics.name: runner-up, runners-up hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use hyphenated forms: runner-up and runners-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: rush hour hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use two words for the noun 'rush hour'; hyphenate the adjective 'rush-hour'.

rubrics_metrics.name: rushed to hospital (avoid cliché)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Rushed to hospital' is a cliché.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'taken to hospital' or 'treated in hospital'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman Catholic Church (titles and Curia guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Official title is 'Roman Catholic Church' though 'Catholic Church' can be used; guidance on hierarchy and usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to the pope as 'Pope [Name]' at first reference, later 'the pope'. Explain Curia if used. Distinguish Vatican (city-state) and Holy See (Church administration) and use terms appropriately. Papal envoys are papal nuncios and their embassies are nunciatures. If no formal diplomatic relations exist, the Pope's envoy is an apostolic delegate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman numerals conversion and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide Roman numeral conversions for reference and use Roman numerals for royalty and past church leaders as specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples shown in reference tables (I, II, III ... XX ... etc.). Use Roman numerals where convention dictates (royalty, historical figures, past popes).

rubrics_metrics.name: sentence length (clarity and translatability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences should generally be short but varied; avoid complex constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sentence with more than one subordinate clause can be hard to follow and difficult to translate.

rubrics_metrics.name: sexist language (avoid stereotypes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use language that perpetuates the stereotype of women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid references to gender, a woman's looks, hairstyle or clothing unless relevant to the story. Avoid sexist references and linguistic absurdities. Use neutral, non-stereotyping language.

rubrics_metrics.name: sharia wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Write 'sharia' (lower case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Sharia law' is tautologous — write 'sharia' or 'Islamic law'.

rubrics_metrics.name: sheikh spelling/usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'sheikh' not 'sheik' or 'shaikh'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Saudi Arabia it may be a courtesy title; elsewhere it can apply to ruling families—use at first reference and avoid casual use.

rubrics_metrics.name: sheriff title capitalisation (U.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalise 'Sheriff' as a title before a name in the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shia usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'Shi'ite' unless in a direct quote.

rubrics_metrics.name: ships' names and national prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use HMS or USS if the nationality of the ship is already clear; omit quotation marks and use neuter pronouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write 'the British frigate Battleaxe' not 'the British frigate HMS Battleaxe' unless in a dateline where 'ABOARD HMS BATTLEAXE' is acceptable. Routinely check names in Jane’s Fighting Ships, Lloyd’s Register. Do not put quotation marks around ship names.

rubrics_metrics.name: shoeshine, shoestring spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'shoeshine' and 'shoestring' as one word.

rubrics_metrics.name: shoo-in spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'shoo-in', not 'shoe-in'.

rubrics_metrics.name: sneaked vs snuck
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'sneaked', not 'snuck'.

rubrics_metrics.name: so as to (use to)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'to' instead of 'so as to'.

rubrics_metrics.name: so-called usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'so-called' as an adjective and adverb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Security capitalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalise when referring to the U.S. system.

rubrics_metrics.name: socialist capitalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalise only when part of a proper name.

rubrics_metrics.name: software naming and quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalise software names without quotation marks; use quotation marks for computer games.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g. Windows, Internet Explorer; games: "Bust a Move: Dance Summit".

rubrics_metrics.name: Somali vs Somalian
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'Somali', not 'Somalian'.

rubrics_metrics.name: some vs about for approximate figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Write 'about 500 people' rather than 'some 500 people'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Some' as an approximation is more likely to confuse translators than 'about'.

rubrics_metrics.name: song title capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalise every word in a song title apart from conjunctions, articles, particles and short prepositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "All You Need Is Love", "Son of a Preacher Man".

rubrics_metrics.name: sophisticated (avoid vagueness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'sophisticated' as a vague 'modish' term; use 'modern' if that's what you mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most weapon systems are 'sophisticated'—if you mean 'modern' say so.

rubrics_metrics.name: spelled vs spelt; regional spelling rules
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two generally accepted spelling systems (American and British). Copy originating in the Americas should follow North American spelling conventions; copy originating elsewhere should follow British spelling norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At all times stick to official spellings for American names and titles (e.g. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates). Watch regional words that translators may find difficult. In American sports coverage use American terms and spellings (center, maneuver, defense, offense, ballclub, postseason, preseason, lineman, line up, halfback, doubleheader).

rubrics_metrics.name: spill spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'spilled' not 'spilt'.

rubrics_metrics.name: spin off vs spinoff
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Spin off' is the verb; 'spinoff' is the noun.

rubrics_metrics.name: spokesman/spokeswoman vs spokesperson
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'spokesman' or 'spokeswoman', not 'spokesperson'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the sex of the person is not known then use 'representative'.

rubrics_metrics.name: spoonful spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'spoonful' and 'spoonfuls', not 'spoonsful' or 'spoons full'.

rubrics_metrics.name: sports events titles and capitalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower case for sport names; use upper case for an event title; use singular or plural 'championships' correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g. French Open tennis championships; use the name of the sport before 'championship', 'tournament' etc.; use singular 'championship' when one title is at stake and plural when more than one.

rubrics_metrics.name: sports metaphors (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using sports metaphors that may confuse or mislead readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: slang (avoid for global audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid slang not readily understood outside the English-speaking world or by translators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a vivid quote contains slang, explain it in brackets or give a paraphrased version.
